course.title: Atomic – Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics — Stage 9

unit.title: Statistical Investigations
unit.blurb: Planning an investigation: populations and samples, sampling methods, sample size, data collection, and spotting and reducing bias.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Select, trial and justify methods to collect data, including sampling a population: random, systematic and proportional (stratified) samples.

O2.t: Choose a suitable sample size and explain how it affects the reliability of conclusions.

O3.t: Identify sources of bias in sampling and in questions, and suggest how to reduce it.

p: The **population** is everyone (or everything) you want to know about. A **sample** is the part you actually ask or measure.
A sample is quicker and cheaper, but it must **represent** the population. Larger samples usually give more **reliable** results.
**Random**: every member has the same chance (e.g. numbered names drawn by a computer).
**Systematic**: choose every kᵗʰ member from a list, e.g. every 10ᵗʰ name, starting at a random point.
**Proportional (stratified)**: split the population into groups and sample each group in proportion to its size.

lesson.q: A school has 360 Stage 7, 300 Stage 8 and 240 Stage 9 students. A sample of 60 is taken in proportion. How many Stage 9 students?

p: **Primary** data you collect yourself; **secondary** data was collected by someone else. **Discrete** data can be counted (number of pets); **continuous** data is measured (height, time).
A sample of 5 people cannot represent a school of 1000 – the results could change a lot by chance. A common guide is at least 10% for small populations, and never fewer than about 30.

p: A sample or question is **biased** if it makes some answers more likely than they should be, so the results do not represent the population.
Common causes: asking only one type of person (e.g. only people at a gym about exercise), **leading questions** ('Don't you agree that…?'), too small a sample, and people choosing whether to reply.

lesson.q: A council asks people in a car park whether a new car park is needed.
steps: people in a car park drive
they are more likely to say yes
lesson.a: Biased – ask a random sample of all residents instead.

p: Use **response boxes** that do not overlap and cover every possible answer, e.g. 0–1, 2–3, 4–5, 6 or more (hours).
Keep questions short, clear and about one thing only.
Boxes 0–2, 2–4, 4–6 overlap: someone who answers 2 could tick two boxes.
